issues.legal_issue: Assistance by a vendor to a pre-emption plaintiff does not, without evidence of a sham or deceitful arrangement, establish collusion that defeats the plaintiff’s right.
material_facts: The plaintiffs were the vendors’ sons and sued to exercise their own right of pre-emption.

The vendors and plaintiffs were found to reside and eat together, and the vendors paid the litigation expenses; a vendor had also obtained a public document used in the suit, and the vendors were seen with the plaintiffs and their counsel at court.

The final court of fact accepted a plaintiff’s evidence that he was pursuing the purchase for himself and using his own earnings, and the defendants produced no sufficient evidence that the suit was fictitious or brought for the vendors’ benefit.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish collusion, and the plaintiffs did not lose their right of pre-emption on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Collusion in judicial proceedings ordinarily involves a secret arrangement under which a fictitious claim and sham contest are used to obtain an apparent judicial decision for a sinister or improper purpose. A pre-emption right is a personal statutory right of substitution; a plaintiff may obtain financial assistance from any source, and a vendor’s assistance to the plaintiff does not, without more, defeat that right. The Court did not decide whether a plaintiff acting as the vendor’s benamidar would lose the right.

rule.if: preemption_suit and vendor_assisted_plaintiff and not evidence_of_sham_or_deceitful_arrangement

predicates.preemption_suit: The proceeding is a suit by a claimant seeking to exercise a right of pre-emption.
predicates.vendor_assisted_plaintiff: The vendor helped the plaintiff pursue the suit or provided assistance connected with it.
predicates.evidence_of_sham_or_deceitful_arrangemen: Evidence shows that the plaintiff and vendor arranged a fictitious claim or sham contest for an improper purpose.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff seeks pre-emption, the vendor assists the plaintiff, and there is no evidence of a sham or deceitful arrangement, the plaintiff’s pre-emption right is not lost for collusion.

issues.legal_issue: Where part of the property sold is held by tenants and the vendees have not taken physical possession of the whole property, the registration-based starting point applies to limitation for a pre-emption suit.
material_facts: A tenant was cultivating part of the land sold at the time of the sale.
The vendees had not taken physical possession of the whole property on the date of sale.
The suit was filed within the limitation period calculated from registration of the sale deed.
issues.conclusion: The first part of Article 10 did not apply because the vendees had not taken physical possession of the whole property; the second part applied, making the suit timely from the date of registration.
issues.legal_principle: Article 10 of the Second Schedule to the Limitation Act, 1908, provides a one-year period for a pre-emption suit, beginning when the purchaser takes physical possession of the whole property sold, or, where the subject of the sale does not admit of physical possession, when the sale instrument is registered. Physical possession means personal and immediate possession, as explained in Batut Begam v. Mansur Ali Khan (I.L.R. 24 All. 17) and applied in Ghulam Mustafa v. Shahabuddin (49 P.R. 1908). Section 30 of the Punjab Pre-emption Act applies only where the case does not fall within Article 10.

predicates.preemption_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking to enforce a right of pre-emption.
predicates.part_of_property_held_by_tenants: At the relevant time, tenants held part of the property that was sold.
predicates.vendees_lacked_physical_possession_of_wh: The purchasers had not taken personal and immediate possession of the whole property sold.
predicates.suit_filed_within_registration_based_lim: The suit was filed within the applicable limitation period measured from registration of the sale instrument.

issues.definition: If a pre-emption suit concerns property partly held by tenants, the purchasers lack physical possession of the whole property, and the suit is filed within the registration-based limit, the suit is within limitation.
